newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communists say Yeltsin overestimates power.
newsitem.headline: Communists say Yeltsin overestimates power.

text.p: Russian communists said on Monday President Boris Yeltsin had proved he was out of contact with reality in threatening his opponents with tough retaliation if they attempted to ease him from power.

Yeltsin, who had heart surgery last November, appeared in public on Sunday for the first time since a bout of pneumonia last month in what was clearly intended as a demonstration of his readiness for the political fray.
Asked about attempts by the opposition-dominated parliament to remove him on health grounds, Yeltsin growled:
"They should know I am a fighter and I remain a fighter. They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back."

Yeltsin did not elaborate and kept to the lexicon of politics. The communists, however, clearly took his words as a reference to 1993 when he set the constitution aside and ordered the Soviet-era parliament to dissolve, accusing deputies of stalling reforms.

When they refused to obey and supporters staged a bloody rebellion in Moscow, Yeltsin brought tanks into the capital and battered the White House parliament building into submission. The army, however, hesitated to intervene in politics.
Gennady Zyuganov, whose communist party holds sway in the parliament set up by Yeltsin with limited powers to replace the old legislature, told reporters:
'He should have chosen different words after such a serious illness and after what he has done to the country."
"I do not think his threat is realistic and neither the army nor the people will support him," said Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in last July's presidential election.
Viktor Ilyukhin, communist chairman of the security committee in the State Duma lower house, told reporters he was "dispirited" by Yeltsin's remarks.
"The president is unable to evaluate the situation in the country realistically," Ilyukhin said.
"I am not surprised by his threat because this man has never recognised the constitution," said Ilyukhin, who is spearheading attempts to unseat Yeltsin for health reasons.
Zyuganov advocates constitutional changes to redistribute powers in favour of the government and parliament but such amendments are unlikely to become law.
